**Highest-value next step, more true now than before:** the Figma comment thread on this exact
screen (Charmaine's note, ~2026-07-30, tagging Kiera + the user, **1 reply already posted**)
is now confirmed to likely be the *only* record of this decision anywhere — Jira and
Confluence have both been exhaustively searched and come back empty. Reading that reply
directly is worth more than further repo/Jira/Confluence digging at this point.

**Update 2026-08-11 (MS Copilot sweep of Teams/Outlook) — the single most valuable finding of
the whole investigation, and it changes the bottom line.** Per a Teams thread in "ZIMM - PM/BA
Team", **Friday 7 Aug 2026** (Tim Lavelle, Jasmijn Tsang, Isabel Chaloner):
- Tim Lavelle: "Do you know where I can view the book an appointment functionality on the zimm
  site?" → Jasmijn Tsang: "I dont think you can today right? Design's for future scope I
  think" → **Isabel Chaloner: "Noo, booking appointments was agreed in scope for go-live via
  Booxi. They were supposed to go live on Magento before, but Emma has now told me that it
  won't be live on Magento. They don't currently seem to have clear timelines on this, and
  sitting with marketing team."** → Tim Lavelle: "Right, ok - we'll need to have a session with
  Booxi on implementation approach. I will send an email."

**This confirms in-storefront Booxi booking (not just history) IS agreed in scope for
go-live** — more definite than Confluence/Jira's "TBC" framing. But **the implementation
approach (widget vs. custom UI vs. API) was explicitly still unresolved as of 7 Aug**, four
days before Kiera's question — Tim was arranging a dedicated session with Booxi specifically
to settle it. No record of that session happening, or of Tim's promised follow-up email,
turned up anywhere Copilot could search. **So Kiera's question is a genuinely live, unanswered
open question as of today, not something anyone dropped the ball on.**

**People — corrected/completed via Copilot (Teams/Outlook directory, more current than
Confluence/Jira rosters):**
- **Charmaine Lew** — title is **Visual Design Manager** (Melbourne), not "Product Designer" as
  Confluence's roster listed — a more senior title; same person, same design authority.
- **Kiera Rikard-Bell** — **Digital Product Design Specialist**, based in **Canberra** (resolves
  the "role unknown" gap from the Confluence/Jira pass). She's an **attendee of today's "[Sprint
  3] Components, components, components" meeting** (11:00 AM, organiser Natasha Lay/Tash —
  the same meeting from earlier in this session — alongside Tim Lavelle, Isabel Chaloner,
  Bianca Morley, Jasmijn Tsang, and the user). Very likely why she asked today: probably
  chasing context ahead of/around that meeting, not out of the blue.

**Booxi vs. Booksy — now definitively resolved, and a real contract-level issue found.** Hardi
Sempuno corrected this explicitly in Teams on **27 May 2026**: *"'Booksy' → 'Booxi'. Wrong
vendor name (Booxi is the appointments platform; Booksy is unrelated). Ref: account.md
CRM-165."* So Booxi is confirmed correct, Booksy confirmed wrong — but **the error was never
fully corrected and persists in the signed SOW** ("2026.07.21 - Zimmermann x Accenture -
Implementation SOW - Execution copy.docx"), which lists "Booksy" among **out-of-scope
third-party vendors for build/configuration** — meaning Accenture builds the PWA-side
integration to the vendor's endpoint but does **not** configure the vendor's own platform
(so if the widget-embed path is chosen, wiring it in is dev work, but configuring Booxi itself
— business hours, staff, availability rules — is Zimmermann's own responsibility, not this
team's). Worth flagging as a genuine, if minor, contract-hygiene issue, separate from the
calendar question itself.

**Other confirmed, consistent with everything above:** a 9 Jul Teams message (Jasmijn Tsang)
already flagged Booxi missing from the Confluence integration register — Hardi Sempuno replied
"It is in my TSD (just FYI)," implying a more detailed Hardi-authored Booxi TSD may exist
outside Confluence (not yet located). Isabel Chaloner was chasing Booxi API/vendor docs as of
22 Jun. No Teams/Outlook message anywhere names a specific calendar library or the Booxi
Booking Widget as a chosen approach — full alignment with the Jira/Confluence findings above.
Figma comment-reply content (including the "1 reply" on this exact screen) does not reliably
reach Outlook/Teams at all — confirmed by Copilot finding only an unrelated 23 Jul Figma-comment
email (a 32px margin note, different file: "Zimmermann_Design_System_2026") — so opening Figma
directly remains the only way to see that reply.

Related: [[reference_confluence_sfcc]], [[project_real_sprint_cadence]].

content.thinking:
A project rules file for Squad A just appeared in my context, which covers the header component I'm currently working on. This seems to be a legitimate system file surfacing relevant guidelines for the territory I'm in, not an injection attempt. The header is a Tier 2 shared shell component that requires Squad A and Squad B coordination if changes are made, which is useful context for implementation but not something I need to surface in my response to Kiera since she's asking for a design opinion, not a delivery plan. Let me refocus on her actual question about the header and bag icon.

Looking at the current implementation, I can see the desktop version already displays a numeric count next to "Bag" in parentheses when there are items in the cart, while mobile uses a badge overlay on the basket icon — so the mobile experience is already implementing the numbered badge pattern that Kiera was asked to mock up. The icon itself doesn't have any filled or changed state logic; it's purely the badge and text count that appear conditionally based on cart contents. So the real question here is whether a numbered badge actually solves the problem well, or if there are genuine UX/technical friction points that make Kiera's alternative (filled icon state without a number) worth considering instead. Let me think through what could actually go wrong with the badge approach.

The data itself isn't a blocker — `useCurrentBasket` already gives us `totalItems` from the commerce SDK, so the infrastructure to power a count is already there and reactive. But the visual side gets trickier: a number badge changes the spatial footprint of the icon, which means either reserving space for it (affecting the header layout) or handling edge cases like "9+" for double-digit counts, and that's where the design friction starts to show.

Accessibility is actually fine — the existing `aria-label` on the IconButton already exposes the item count to screen readers properly. The real gotcha is the SSR hydration mismatch: since `totalItems` comes from a client-side React Query fetch, the server-rendered version won't have that data on first paint, which could cause a flash or layout shift when the client hydrates. I'm also considering whether `totalItems` represents a count of distinct line items or the sum of all quantities across them — for instance, two units of the same product could show as "1" or "2" depending on how it's calculated. The SDK typically sums quantities across all line items, which is the standard commerce behavior, so this is more of a clarification point for Kiera than an actual problem. Overall, the numbered badge approach seems like the safer choice since it aligns with how the current implementation already works. The filled-state approach is visually cleaner but loses the "how many items" signal that reassures shoppers about their cart contents—especially valuable for luxury goods where a few expensive items matter more than quantity. It's really a UX trade-off between simplicity and transparency rather than a technical constraint. The numbered badge approach is already baked into the current draft using the existing Basket+Badge pattern, so it's a straightforward, low-risk choice. The key thing to flag regardless of direction is handling high item counts — probably need a cap like "9+" to avoid overflow. And since the filled-state option is technically just as simple (if not simpler) to implement, the real decision here is purely about UX preference, not feasibility constraints on either side.

Now I should check those specific Figma node IDs against JIRA to see if there's already a ticket or decision documented about the bag icon behavior, particularly in SFCC-52 where the Global Header UI requirements should live.…

content.text:
Found it — and this changes the answer meaningfully. SFCC-52's own Acceptance Criteria (the Global Header UI ticket, "Ready for Development") explicitly states: *"Given a shopper has items in their bag, when they view the header, then the Bag icon displays the correct running count of items"* and *"...the Bag icon count updates without requiring a full page reload."* Confluence's confirmed requirements independently say the same thing (HPC-021: "Bag icon displays running item count"), and it's echoed again in SFCC-315 (the cart overlay header). This isn't an open design question — the numbered count is a **signed-off requirement**, and it's already how the current draft header is built (mobile has a `Badge` with the count over the basket icon; desktop shows "Bag (3)" as text).

## For you

No technical issues with the numbered approach — if anything it's the lower-risk option since it's already spec'd, already wired to live basket data (`useCurrentBasket`), and partially implemented. The one open detail nobody's defined yet: what happens at high counts (does 12 or 127 ever cap/truncate to something like "9+"?) — worth a decision either way, not a blocker. Her simpler "filled icon, no number" idea is also perfectly buildable, but it would mean revisiting a requirement that's already been signed off (HPC-021), not just picking between two undecided options — worth you knowing that distinction before this goes further.

## Redrafted reply for Kiera

```
Hey Kiera!

No issues on the technical side — and it's actually more settled than a "proposed state": the running item count on the bag icon is a signed-off requirement already, not just a design preference. It's also already partly built that way in the current header (a number badge on mobile, "Bag (3)" text on desktop).

One small thing worth designing for regardless: what the badge looks like at higher counts — e.g. does 12 or 127 ever need to cap or truncate (like showing "9+"), since right now it'd just render whatever the real number is.

If you still want to push your simpler filled-icon version, worth knowing that'd mean revisiting an existing signed-off requirement rather than choosing between two open options — good to go in with that context either way!
```

Confirmed with a proper check (not just the earlier surface read): **no, the cap/truncation question hasn't been decided anywhere.** I ran it down three ways —

- **HPC-021** (the confirmed requirement) just says "displays running item count," full stop.
- **SFCC-52's Acceptance Criteria** says "displays the correct running count of items" and "updates without requiring a full page reload" — again, no cap logic specified.
- **SFCC-315** (cart overlay) just says "dynamic item count."
- The **current draft code** renders `{totalItems}` directly into the `Badge` with zero truncation logic, and the header theme file (`header.ts`) has no badge-specific sizing/overflow rule that would hint at an assumed max width.
- I ran a full-text sweep across the whole project for "cap"/"truncat"/"9+"/"99+" — the only real hit was SFCC-649, and that's about capping *purchase quantity per SKU* (a completely different concept), not the header badge's display format.

So your read is exactly right — the "headache" isn't building a number, it's that nobody's actually specified what happens past single digits, and that's a genuine gap someone needs to close before this can be built cleanly either way.

On the filled-icon point — I think you're onto something real, not just a hunch. Filled-vs-outline as a "you are here" signal is about as close to a universal convention as icon states get (tab bars, sidebars, top nav — the filled one is almost always read as "current/active," not "has contents"). It also matters *why* that convention exists: filled/outline toggles map naturally onto states the *user* directly flips (wishlist heart, active nav item) — a single, user-controlled binary. Cart-has-items is a system-computed, multi-value state, which is a worse semantic fit for that pattern, and it's probably why virtually every major retailer (luxury ones included) puts an actual number on the bag icon rather than a fill toggle — it's the only zero-learning-curve way to convey "there's stuff in here, and here's how much" without expecting a shopper to learn a bespoke convention on the spot. So I'd treat that as a real strike against the filled-only option, not just a stylistic quibble.
